strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies a genuine limitation of current localization agents (treating every instance as memoryless) and connects it to how human developers accumulate repository expertise, supported by a convincing motivating failure case (Figure 2).

The proposed mechanism is lightweight, modular, and well-specified: two complementary memory stores (episodic memory of commits/issues with BM25-based SearchCommit/ExamineCommit, and semantic memory of LLM summaries for actively-edited files) integrate cleanly into an existing SOTA framework (LocAgent) without modifying it.

Careful experimental hygiene: commits made after the issue's base commit are excluded, and instances with overlapping text or linked issues are filtered to prevent leakage—a contamination risk often overlooked in SWE-bench-style augmentation work.

Solid evaluation with appropriate baselines spanning retrieval-based (CodeRankEmbed), procedural (Agentless), and agentic (LocAgent) approaches, plus component-level ablations showing both memory types contribute and combine positively on two benchmarks.

Thoughtful analyses that go beyond headline numbers: per-repository breakdown correlating gains with commit-history richness (including honest reporting of a -13.1 regression on history-poor repos), tool-use distribution shifts, per-example cost scatter analysis revealing the heterogeneous cost-effectiveness trade-off, and a retrieval-method comparison (sparse BM25 beating dense retrieval) with a plausible explanation.
Paper is well written and clearly organized, with useful appendix documentation of the tool interfaces for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core method reduces to BM25 retrieval over commit messages plus LLM-generated summaries of the most-edited files, i.e., conventional RAG over an additional data source. The conceptual contribution ('give agents repository memory via commit history') is intuitive and the mechanisms are straightforward, making the work feel incremental relative to the memory-augmented agent literature it cites (e.g., Chen et al. 2025a, Wang et al. 2025c).

Narrow validation of generality: the memory is integrated only into LocAgent and evaluated with a single backbone (GPT-4o). Claims about the value of repository memory would be substantially strengthened by demonstrating gains on at least one additional agentic framework (e.g., OpenHands-style) and one more LLM.

Benchmark limitations: SWE-bench-live evaluation uses a small filtered subset (130 examples across 62 repositories), making per-metric differences of a few points less statistically robust; no significance testing or variance analysis across runs is reported for the agentic experiments.

The regression on history-poor repositories is acknowledged but not resolved—the paper offers no adaptive mechanism to decide when memory should be used, deferring this to future work, so the method can actively hurt on a meaningful class of instances.

Hyperparameters of the memory construction (7,000 commits, top-200 files) are fixed without sensitivity analysis, and it is unclear how sensitive results are to these choices or how the approach transfers to repositories with different commit-message conventions.
No explicit statement about code/data release, which limits reproducibility of the memory pipeline despite the appendix tool documentation.

strengths: The core motivation is clear and well-articulated: existing agentic localization frameworks treat every issue as a fresh puzzle, while human developers accumulate long-term repository knowledge. Framing commit history as a natural source of episodic and semantic memory is intuitive and well-motivated.

The method is lightweight and modular, and the paper demonstrates this by cleanly integrating the four memory tools (SearchCommit, ExamineCommit, ViewSummary, SearchSummary) into an existing SOTA framework (LocAgent) without modifying its core loop.
The paper reports useful ablations: episodic-only and semantic-only variants both contribute, and the combined setting is best, supporting the complementarity claim.

The analysis sections add value beyond the headline numbers: per-repository breakdown correlating gains with commit history volume (Table 2), tool-use distribution shift (Figure 3), per-example cost analysis (Figure 4/Table 3), and a comparison of sparse vs. dense retrieval for the memory interface (Table 4).
Contamination handling is explicitly addressed: only commits predating the issue's base commit are included, and text-overlapping issues/linked commits are filtered out.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the contribution is essentially BM25-based retrieval over commit messages plus LLM-generated file summaries exposed as agent tools. This is a fairly straightforward application of RAG/tool augmentation to a new data source (commit history), and the connection to the broader 'memory-augmented agent' literature (e.g., Agent Workflow Memory, Chen et al. 2025a) is only superficially explored. No training, learning, or adaptive memory mechanism is proposed.

Single framework integration: all experiments are on LocAgent only. The claim that memory tools 'integrate easily into existing frameworks' is not empirically supported—no results with Agentless, SWE-agent, OpenHands, or any other agentic framework.

Single backbone LLM (GPT-4o 2024-05-13, an older snapshot) with no repetition runs, variance estimates, or statistical significance tests, despite the agentic setting being highly stochastic. Some reported gains (e.g., +1.6 Acc@1 on SWE-bench-live) are small and could fall within run-to-run noise.

The SWE-bench-live evaluation is on a small filtered subset (130 examples, instances requiring ≤5 file changes, 62 repositories), which limits the generality and statistical power of the comparison; the filtering criteria differ from how the baseline numbers are typically reported.

A notable failure mode is left unaddressed: on low-history repositories ('others' group), RepoMem degrades performance substantially (-13.1 Acc@5 vs. LocAgent). The paper acknowledges this but offers no mitigation (e.g., confidence-based gating of memory usage), which weakens the practical value of the method.

Potential data-leakage subtleties are not fully examined: semantic memory summaries are generated by an LLM from the repository state, but it is unclear whether summaries could be built from code snapshots that postdate the issue's base commit; similarly, the filtering threshold for 'overlapping text' with test instances is not specified or analyzed.

Reproducibility is limited: no code/data release is mentioned, key hyperparameters (top-k for retrieval, number of retrieved summaries, prompt templates for the agent) are only partially documented in the appendix, and LLM-generated summaries are not released.

Efficiency analysis is qualitative: the average cost increase is admitted but no aggregate cost-vs-accuracy trade-off summary (e.g., cost per correctly localized example) is provided, and the cost plots use unnormalized API prices.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper identifies a genuine, previously underexplored limitation of agentic code localization frameworks (treated as memoryless), and draws a compelling analogy to how human developers accumulate repository knowledge.

The proposed memory mechanisms (episodic memory of past commits with linked issues, semantic memory of actively evolving files) are simple, lightweight, and modular, making them easy to integrate into existing agentic frameworks; the leakage-prevention steps (excluding commits after the base commit and filtering overlapping text with test instances) are thoughtful and important.

Solid experimental design: comparisons against representative baselines spanning retrieval-based (CodeRankEmbed), procedural (Agentless), and agentic (LocAgent) approaches, on both SWE-bench-verified and the newer SWE-bench-live benchmark, with ablations isolating the contribution of each memory type.

Rich analysis beyond headline numbers: per-repository breakdown correlating gains with commit-history depth, tool-use distribution showing a behavioral shift toward hypothesis-driven investigation, per-instance cost analysis revealing heterogeneous cost effects, and a retrieval-method comparison (BM25 with LLM tokenizer vs. dense retrieval) with a plausible explanation—these add genuine insight.
The paper is well written, with informative figures (failure-case walkthrough in Figure 2, tool documentation in the appendix) that aid reproducibility and understanding.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in methodological depth: the core techniques are straightforward—BM25 over commit messages plus LLM-generated summaries of the top-200 frequently edited files. The contribution is primarily an empirical finding rather than a new technique, which may limit impact.

Gains are modest and inconsistent on SWE-bench-live (+3.1 Acc@5 on a small 130-example subset), and the 'others' group in Table 2 shows a large degradation (-13.1), indicating the method can hurt when history is sparse; no automatic mechanism is proposed to detect and avoid such cases, only suggestions for future work.

Evaluation uses only a single backbone LLM (GPT-4o) and integrates memory into only one framework (LocAgent); broader applicability claims would be better supported with at least one additional agent framework or model.

All results are localization-only (file-level Acc@k); the paper does not measure downstream impact on end-to-end issue resolution, which is the ultimate task of interest, and no statistical significance testing or variance reporting is provided.

Reproducibility is questionable: no mention of released code, crawled commit datasets, or prompts beyond the appendix tool documentation; the SWE-bench-live subset construction (intersection of 'lite' and 'verified' splits) is nonstandard and briefly described.

The distinction between 'episodic' and 'semantic' memory borrows cognitive-science terminology but the mapping is loose; the semantic memory component is essentially a file-level retrieval baseline and its individual contribution (+1.2 Acc@5 over LocAgent) is smaller than the episodic component.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies that current localization agents treat every instance as a fresh problem with no repository knowledge, and proposes a natural remedy grounded in commit history, connecting intuitions from JIT-SDP literature in a sensible way.

The proposed mechanism (episodic memory of past commits + semantic memory of active files via LLM summaries) is simple, lightweight, and modularly integrated into the state-of-the-art LocAgent framework, making it easy to adopt.

Consistent empirical gains across two benchmarks (SWE-bench-verified and SWE-bench-live), with clear ablations showing both memory components contribute (episodic-only and semantic-only each improve over LocAgent), and a convincing end-to-end resolve-rate result (37.0% -> 40.4%).

Thoughtful analyses beyond headline numbers: per-repository breakdown correlating gains with commit-history richness (with honest reporting of degradation on sparse-history repos), tool-use distribution shift, cost cross-comparison showing the extra spend is concentrated on hard cases, retrieval-method ablation (BM25 vs dense), and sensitivity to K.

Attention to contamination/leakage control (commits restricted to pre-issue history, filtering of text-overlapping issues and linked commits), and extensive reproducibility material including tool documentation, example tool outputs, and the agent prompt.
Candid error analysis acknowledging that irrelevant memory can distract the agent and hurt performance in repositories with sparse or irrelevant history.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core method is essentially BM25 retrieval over commit messages plus LLM-generated file summaries for top-edited files, wrapped as ReAct tools. The contribution is more an empirical demonstration of a simple idea than a new technique, and the connection to prior memory-augmented agent work (e.g., Agent Workflow Memory, SWE-Exp) could be more deeply differentiated.

Results are only established with a single backbone LLM (GPT-4o 2024-05-13) and a single host framework (LocAgent). Since the paper claims modularity and general applicability, demonstrating the memory augment on at least one other framework or LLM would substantially strengthen the claims.

The SWE-bench-live evaluation is on a small filtered subset (130 examples, <=5 files to modify), so the ~3-point gains there may be fragile; no statistical significance testing or variance analysis is reported for any of the main results.

Evaluation is only at file-level Acc@k; function/class-level localization (which LocAgent's graph representation targets) is not reported, making it harder to compare against the full LocAgent results.

The fixed 7,000-commit window and K=200 are heuristic choices; while ablations exist for K, the sensitivity of results to the commit window size and the 'others' bucket definition (<10K commits) is not analyzed, and the -13.1 regression on sparse-history repositories is a notable unsolved weakness only partially mitigated.

The leakage filter relies on text overlap between linked issues and the test instance, which is a heuristic; the possibility of near-duplicate historical issues/fixes in memory (a subtle form of contamination that could inflate gains, especially for mature repos like django with 231 of the 500 examples) is not thoroughly validated.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: the 'human-like expert developer' framing is a narrative device not directly validated by any human comparison, and the efficiency discussion relies on qualitative scatter-plot interpretation rather than quantitative summaries.

strengths: The motivation is clear and well-articulated: current localization agents treat every issue as fresh with no repository-level memory, and the failure-case analysis in Figure 2 concretely illustrates the gap relative to experienced developers.

The evaluation includes a reasonable set of baselines (retrieval-based, procedural, agentic), ablations of both memory components, a per-repository breakdown, a cost analysis, and an end-to-end downstream resolution-rate experiment (Table 7), which is more thorough than many agent papers.

The paper is honest about limitations: it reports performance degradation on repositories with sparse history, provides overhead measurements (Appendix A.2), and discusses contamination filtering and missing issue links.
The method is simple, lightweight, and integrates with a state-of-the-art framework, with documented tool interfaces, prompts, and a reproducibility statement.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core contribution reduces to two straightforward retrieval tools: BM25 keyword search over past commit messages (with a simple commit-to-issue link lookup) and LLM-generated summaries for the top-200 most frequently edited files. Both ideas are directly borrowed from the Just-in-Time defect prediction literature ('hotspot' files, commit history as signal, acknowledged by the authors in §2.2), and the memory framing is largely a relabeling of standard RAG over repository metadata. No new learning, memory mechanism, or algorithmic idea is proposed.

Serious risk of test-set tuning and information leakage. The authors explicitly state that the Django repository was their 'primary repository for preliminary analysis and prototyping' (Appendix B.1), yet Django is also the largest and most influential test repository in SWE-bench-verified (231 of 500 examples). The key hyperparameters (K=200 for semantic memory, the LLM-based BM25 tokenizer in Table 4) were selected on the same repository used for evaluation, undermining the reported gains. The ablations in Tables 4 and 5-6 are conducted only on Django rather than held-out repositories.

Contamination concerns with the episodic memory are not adequately resolved. SWE-bench issues are drawn from real repository histories, so prior commits frequently address closely related (or same-root-cause) issues in the same files. The authors' mitigation—filtering issues with 'overlapping text' with the test instance—is vague and weak; near-duplicates, related bug families, and commits touching the exact target files could still act as powerful hints rather than genuine 'memory.' No analysis quantifying how often the retrieved commits directly reveal the ground-truth fix location is provided.

Gains are modest and inconsistent. Acc@5 improves from 71.6 to 76.5 on SWE-bench-verified, but the per-repository breakdown (Table 2) shows the improvement is concentrated in a few repositories (pytest +16.7, sphinx +11.4, django +7.4), no change on astropy, and a large degradation (-13.1) on the 'others' group with limited history. No statistical significance testing is reported for any comparison.

Narrow evaluation scope. The method is integrated only into LocAgent, despite claims that the tools are 'modular' and 'easily integrated into existing frameworks.' Generality to other agentic frameworks (SWE-agent, OpenHands, Agentless) is untested. Only a single backbone LLM (GPT-4o) is used, and only file-level localization is evaluated—no function/class-level metrics despite these being standard in prior work (e.g., LocAgent).
The SWE-bench-live evaluation is on a small, non-standard 130-example subset constructed by the authors, limiting statistical power and comparability with other published results on that benchmark.

Failure analysis is thin. The 'Error Analysis' (§4.3) is a small-scale, qualitative discussion that mostly restates the observations already evident from Table 2. The proposed future direction (agents deciding when to use memory) is left unexplored, so the known failure mode of memory misleading the agent on low-history repositories remains unaddressed in the method itself.

Several design choices are under-motivated heuristics (7,000-commit window, top-200 files, commit-message-only matching despite acknowledged noisy/missing issue links), and the impact of these choices is evaluated only on the prototyping repository.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: augmenting agentic localization frameworks with repository-specific memory derived from commit history (episodic memory of past commits/issues, semantic memory of actively evolving files) is a sensible and underexplored direction, supported by a convincing motivating failure case (Figure 2).
The method is simple, modular, and easy to integrate; the paper demonstrates this concretely by plugging the memory tools into LocAgent with no changes to its core toolset or prompt.

Evaluation is reasonably thorough: consistent gains over LocAgent on both SWE-bench-verified (+4.9 Acc@5) and SWE-bench-live, with ablations isolating the contribution of each memory type, a per-repository breakdown that validates the core hypothesis (rich history → larger gains), cost analysis (Table 3, Figure 4), retrieval-method ablation (BM25 vs. dense), sensitivity analysis over K, and an end-to-end resolution-rate check (Table 7) showing localization gains translate downstream.
Good operational analysis: offline construction time and online latency overhead are quantified, showing the memory adds negligible runtime cost.
Reproducibility is addressed seriously: memory construction details, prompts, tool documentation, and example outputs are provided in appendices, and code release is promised.
Contamination risks are considered explicitly (memory restricted to commits prior to the issue, filtering of overlapping text).
weaknesses: Technical novelty is modest. The episodic memory is essentially BM25 keyword retrieval over commit messages plus a commit-detail lookup, and the semantic memory is an LLM summarization of the top-k most edited files. The connection to JIT-SDP 'hotspots' is acknowledged, and memory-augmented agents are an active area, so the contribution is more a well-executed application than a conceptual advance.

Generality is under-tested: all experiments use a single backbone (GPT-4o 2024-05-13) and a single host framework (LocAgent). The claim that memory tools 'integrate easily into existing frameworks' is plausible but not empirically demonstrated; results with a second backbone or second agentic framework would substantially strengthen the paper.

Results on SWE-bench-live (the more diverse, recent benchmark) are weaker (66.2 vs. 63.1 Acc@5, and Acc@1 gain of only 1.6), and the SWE-bench-live subset is small (130 examples), so some headline gains may not be statistically robust; no significance testing is reported.

The method can hurt performance on repositories with sparse history (Table 2, -13.1 for 'others'), and the paper offers no adaptive mechanism to decide when to rely on memory; this reliability limitation is deferred to future work rather than addressed.

The hyperparameter K=200 was selected using the Django repository, which is also part of the evaluation set, introducing a mild tuning-on-eval concern, and the fixed window of 7,000 commits is a heuristic without sensitivity analysis.
Episodic memory relies on explicit commit-issue links, which are known to be noisy/missing; the paper acknowledges this limits recall but does not quantify its impact.
The error analysis (Section 4.3) is admittedly 'small-scale' and largely qualitative; a more systematic characterization of failure modes would be valuable.
